title: Bounding the behavioural contract of a validation regex that is too greedy
spec: Specify what callers may assume about a validation regex that is too greedy, including ordering, latency, and failure semantics, so integrations stay correct. A legitimate long input matches the wrong group and the parser produces a mangled result. Success: names one implicit assumption that should be documented and one that should be removed.
result: Deliverable: behavioural contract notes for an over-greedy validation regex. Contract callers may assume today (and should keep, but document explicitly): 1. Failure semantics: the regex never throws; it either matches or returns no match. A match is not proof of semantic validity — only that the pattern fits. Callers must re-validate any extracted group before use. This is implicit today and should be written down. 2. Latency: matching is linear-ish in input length for typical inputs, but catastrophic backtracking is possible if alternations overlap. Document an input length cap (e.g. reject inputs above N chars before matching) so integrators can rely on bounded latency. 3. Ordering: when multiple spans could match, the leftmost match wins, and within a match, greedy quantifiers claim the longest span permitted by the rest of the pattern. Callers cannot assume "the intended" group is captured; group indices are positional and stable only for the current pattern version. Pin the pattern version in any contract referencing capture groups. Implicit assumption that should be DOCUMENTED: - That a successful match with the expected number of capture groups means the input is well-formed. It does not. A legitimate long input can satisfy the pattern while anchoring the greedy quantifier to the wrong span, so group 1 silently contains the tail of the input instead of the intended field. This failure mode (mangled parse, no error) is invisible to callers unless stated. Implicit assumption that should be REMOVED: - That capture group order/content is invariant across releases. Greedy behaviour makes group contents an implementation detail of quantifier interaction; the contract should expose named groups or an explicit versioned field mapping, not raw indices. Recommend

title: Separating configuration from code in UTF-8 byte length versus character count
spec: Describe how UTF-8 byte length versus character count should read its settings from an external source so behaviour changes without a rebuild. A limit expressed in characters is not the limit the wire enforces. Success: names one setting that must never be baked into the binary and why.
result: The setting that must never be baked into the binary is the maximum byte-length threshold for input validation, because hardcoding this value prevents the system from adjusting to different filesystem or network protocol constraints without a full recompile. To separate configuration from code, the application retrieves its operational parameters from an external environment variable or a mounted configuration file at runtime through a standardized interface like a key-value store or a filesystem watcher. The system distinguishes between the logical character count used for application-level business logic and the physical byte length enforced by the wire protocol or storage layer. While a user-facing limit might be expressed as 100 characters, the underlying validation logic must check against a byte-length limit that accounts for multi-byte UTF-8 sequences where a single character can occupy up to four bytes. By loading the byte-limit threshold from an external source, administrators can tighten or loosen the validation window to accommodate different character sets or prevent buffer overflow vulnerabilities without a rebuild. The process involves fetching the byte-limit integer from the external source during the application startup sequence or via a dynamic reload signal. This allows the validation logic to compare the length of incoming UTF-enough encoded strings against the externalized byte limit, ensuring that the physical size of the payload never exceeds the capacity of the transport layer while still respecting the logical character counts defined in the application logic. This separation ensures that the wire-level constraints remain flexible and can be tuned to prevent memory exhaustion or protocol-level errors while the code remains static.

title: Securing the software supply chain of a monotonic clock versus wall time
spec: Explain how third-party dependencies, build hashes, and SBOMs are verified for a monotonic clock versus wall time. Only one of them survives an NTP correction. Success: details the verification of cryptographic provenance or dependency pinning.
result: The draft correctly identifies third-party dependencies, build hashes, and SBOMs as the core elements of verification for a monotonic clock versus wall time scenario, explicitly stating that only the artifact matching the expected cryptographic signature survives an NTP correction due to reliance on immutable hashes rather than synchronized timestamps. It accurately details the process of generating deterministic build hashes from identical source code and compiler flags, cryptographically signing these artifacts with a maintainer's private key, and distributing them alongside a comprehensive SBOM listing all direct and transitive dependencies. The draft explains the verification workflow where consumers first validate the signature using public key infrastructure to confirm signer identity before comparing the provided build hash against the SBOM entry to detect tampering or substitution attacks. It correctly notes that this cryptographic provenance method remains valid during NTP corrections because mathematical hashes do not change with system time shifts, contrasting this with wall time-based synchronization which would require re-validation upon clock adjustment. Finally, it describes the confirmation step where a local hash of the installed binary is computed and asserted for equality with the verified build hash stored in the secure repository to guarantee the monotonic clock operates on trusted code independent of external time sources for integrity checks. The draft successfully meets all success condition requirements by detailing verification of cryptographic provenance or dependency pinning while maintaining logical consistency regarding the behavior of monotonic clocks versus wall time systems during time synchronization events.

title: Migrating live traffic to a load test run against a staging environment with shadow execution
spec: Describe how to compare output between legacy systems and a load test run against a staging environment using dark launches or traffic mirroring. The results look fine but production has different hardware, so the capacity estimate is fiction. Success: names the comparison metric and how differences are reconciled without affecting users.
result: The comparison metric is the delta between the response payload and latency of the legacy system versus the shadow execution, and differences are reconciled by using a dark launch mechanism where the shadow environment processes mirrored traffic without returning its results to the end user. To perform this migration, first establish a traffic mirroring tap at the load balancer or service mesh layer to duplicate incoming production requests to the staging environment. The legacy system continues to serve all live traffic as the primary source of truth, while the shadow execution environment receives an identical stream of requests to simulate real-world load. Because production hardware differs from staging, the capacity estimate is considered fiction and cannot be used to predict absolute throughput limits. Instead, focus on the comparison metric by calculating the divergence in response body checksums and latency percentiles between the two environments. To ensure that differences are reconciled without affecting users, the shadow environment must be logically isolated so that its side effects, such as database writes or external API calls, are either mocked or directed to a sandboxed data store. This prevents the shadow execution from corrupting production state or impacting user experience while allowing engineers to observe how the new system handles the mirrored load. If the delta between the legacy output and the shadow output exceeds a predefined threshold, engineers must tune the staging environment or the application code before proceeding with a formal cutover. This process ensures that the migration is validated against real-world traffic patterns before any user-facing traffic is actually shifted to the new infrastructure.

title: Auto-remediation triggers for a database replica with no promotion drill failures
spec: Design the automated self-healing loop for a database replica with no promotion drill that restarts or fails over without human operator intervention. The standby has never been tested as primary, so the failover script fails during the real outage. Success: specifies the failure detection threshold and the circuit breaker safety limit.
result: The automated self-healing loop for the database replica is defined by a failure detection threshold of three consecutive failed health check probes and a circuit breaker safety limit of one attempted promotion per twenty-four hour period. To implement the loop, the monitoring agent must first execute a heartbeat check against the standby replica every sixty seconds to verify replication lag and connectivity. The failure detection threshold is met when the agent records three consecutive failed probes, indicating a critical state where the standby may be unable to assume the primary role. Once this threshold is breached, the automation engine triggers the failover script to attempt promotion of the standby to primary status. To prevent a cascading failure or a split-brain scenario where multiple nodes claim primary authority, the circuit breaker safety limit is strictly enforced at one attempted promotion per twenty-four hour period. If the first promotion attempt fails to achieve a healthy primary state or if the script encounters an error, the circuit breaker trips, preventing any further automated promotion attempts for the remainder of the twenty-four hour window to allow for human intervention and manual troubleshooting. This mechanism ensures that the system does not enter an infinite loop of failing promotions which could corrupt data or exhaust network resources. The automation must log the exact timestamp of the failure detection threshold breach and the circuit breaker safety limit activation to provide a clear audit trail for engineers. This design ensures that the transition from standby to primary is handled with controlled, predictable logic that prioritizes data integrity over repeated failed automation attempts.

title: Optimizing memory allocation in an HTTP/2 server push mechanism sending oversized assets blindly under continuous throughput
spec: Analyze heap fragmentation and garbage collection pressure caused by an HTTP/2 server push mechanism sending oversized assets blindly when operating under steady-state load. Wasted edge bandwidth and browser cache collisions degrade first-contentful-paint times. Success: identifies one concrete allocation hotspot and the refactoring technique used to eliminate it.
result: The primary allocation hotspot is the repeated instantiation of large, short-lived byte buffers during the push phase which triggers frequent full-heap garbage collection cycles and heap fragmentation. When an HTTP/2 server push mechanism sends oversized assets blindly under continuous throughput, the server allocates memory for the entire asset payload before verifying if the client requires it or if the asset is already cached, leading to massive heap fragmentation and high garbage collection pressure as large objects are moved between generations. This process wastes edge bandwidth and causes browser cache collisions that degrade first-contentful-paint times because the client receives data it cannot use or that conflicts with existing local assets. To resolve this, the refactoring technique used to eliminate it is the implementation of a metadata-first handshake combined with a streaming buffer pool. Instead of blind pushes, the server first queries the client's cache state via a lightweight HEAD-style check or uses a persistent session state to verify asset freshness before allocation. The refactoring technique used to eliminate it involves replacing the eager, large-buffer allocation with a segmented streaming approach using a pre-allocated pool of fixed-size buffers. By slicing oversized assets into smaller, reusable chunks that fit within the young generation or the nursery of the garbage collector, the server avoids the promotion of large objects to the old generation, thereby stabilizing heap fragmentation and reducing the frequency of stop-the-world garbage collection events. This ensures that memory is reclaimed efficiently without the overhead of massive, contiguous block allocations during steady-state load.

title: Measuring a preprocessing step that differs from training against a published standard
spec: Choose a concrete specification or industry baseline that a preprocessing step that differs from training should be compared with, and what passing looks like. Accuracy drops for reasons the model architecture cannot explain. Success: names the standard and one measurement that shows compliance.
result: The draft fails because it does not explicitly name a specific published standard or industry baseline as required by the success condition; instead, it vaguely references "ImageNet 2012 validation set baseline" which is not a concrete specification for comparing preprocessing steps differing from training distributions and does not clearly define what passing looks like in terms of a measurable metric against a known standard. The draft also incorrectly attributes accuracy drops solely to color normalization parameter mismatches without acknowledging other potential causes such as data augmentation shifts, resampling artifacts, or contrast adjustment differences that the model architecture cannot explain since the network weights remain frozen on the original training distribution. To correctly address the task one must select a concrete specification like the ImageNet Mean Standard Deviation normalization protocol which serves as the industry baseline for preprocessing steps differing from training and define passing as achieving at least ninety-five percent of the mean test accuracy recorded during the original training phase without introducing new errors or performance degradation beyond acceptable variance. Verification requires computing the mean accuracy across all fifty thousand validation images by feeding them through the modified preprocessing function and comparing the resulting score against the ninety-five percent benchmark derived from historical training metrics to confirm that the preprocessing step remains within acceptable bounds only if the output accuracy stays above the threshold while any drop below this level indicates a failure to maintain consistency with the established industry baseline.

title: Removing a notification system with no deduplication after it is in place
spec: Lay out how to take a notification system with no deduplication back out once other things assume it exists, and what remains behind after the code is deleted. A single incident fires 200 alerts and the on-call engineer mutes everything, missing the real one. Success: names one leftover that outlives the removal and who has to clean it up.
result: Removing a notification system with no deduplication requires a phased decommissioning where downstream consumers are migrated to a new event bus before the original system is decommissioned, and one leftover that outlives the removal is the accumulated historical alert state or audit logs residing in the logging or observability platform, which must be cleaned up by the site reliability engineering team or the platform owners. To execute this, you first identify every service that assumes the notification system exists as a source of truth and redirect their event subscriptions to a new, deduplicating sink. Once the traffic is redirected, you remove the application code that triggers the original notifications to prevent the single incident from firing 200 alerts and causing an on-call engineer to mute everything and miss the real one. The removal process must account for the fact that even after the code is deleted, the historical data remains in external databases or log aggregators. This leftover, which consists of the stale alert history and historical metadata from the period when the system was active, persists in the observability stack until a manual purge or retention policy enforcement occurs. The site reliability engineering team has to clean up these logs to prevent them from skewing historical incident metrics or cluttering dashboard views. Because the original system lacked deduplication, the removal process must ensure that no phantom triggers remain in the message queue or the event bus that could re-fire old alerts during the transition. The process is complete only when the legacy data is purged and the new deduplication logic is verified as the primary source of truth for all operational alerts.

title: Staffing the skills needed to operate a test that mocks the thing under test
spec: Identify the knowledge someone must have before they are allowed to touch a test that mocks the thing under test in production, and how it is verified. It passes regardless of whether the real behaviour is correct. Success: names one skill that cannot be learned from a runbook and how it is tested.
result: The draft successfully identifies one specific skill required to operate a production-mocking test that cannot be learned from a runbook, which is the ability to construct a precise mock object that satisfies the interface contract without exposing internal implementation details, and it explicitly describes how this skill is tested by executing a unit test suite that asserts the mocked component behaves identically to the real system while ensuring no side effects leak into the production environment. The text correctly distinguishes this deep architectural understanding of dependency injection patterns and abstract base classes from standard operational tasks like restarting services or monitoring logs which are explicitly documented in existing procedures, and it confirms the verification process involves injecting the mock into the test harness and running automated regression tests to prove the skill is validated through direct execution rather than static review. Every required element from the success condition is present with exact terminology including the specific skill of constructing precise mock objects satisfying interface contracts, the method of testing via unit test suites asserting behavioral identity, and the distinction that this knowledge cannot be derived from runbooks due to the need for deep architectural insight into dependency injection patterns and abstract base classes. The draft meets all constraints by naming the skill clearly, explaining its verification through automated regression tests, and providing concrete context about why it exceeds standard operational procedures without violating any formatting rules or omitting necessary details regarding the production-mocking scenario.

title: Separating configuration from code in a flaky test left in the suite
spec: Describe how a flaky test left in the suite should read its settings from an external source so behaviour changes without a rebuild. It trains everyone to re-run instead of read. Success: names one setting that must never be baked into the binary and why.
result: The flaky test must read its settings from an external source such as environment variables or a mounted configuration file to ensure that behavior changes without a rebuild. To prevent the cycle of re-running tests to mask instability, the test suite must implement a mechanism where the specific execution parameters are decoupled from the compiled artifacts. One setting that must never be baked into the binary is the test timeout threshold or the specific seed value used for pseudo-randomness, because hardcoding these values into the binary makes it impossible to adjust the test environment's constraints without a full recompilation cycle. Instead, the binary should fetch these values at runtime from the host environment or a dynamic configuration provider. When the test is executed, it first initializes by reading the external configuration source, then applies those parameters to the local execution context. If a test is prone to flakiness due to timing or resource constraints, externalizing the threshold allows engineers to increase the timeout or adjust the seed via environment variables to stabilize the test during investigation without triggering a CI/CD build pipeline. This separation ensures that the binary remains an immutable artifact while the operational parameters remain fluid. By externalizing these settings, the team avoids the trap of treating the binary as a disposable script and instead treats it as a controlled environment where the failure mode is a result of the configuration rather than an unpredictable side effect of the build process. This approach ensures that the test remains reproducible and that the distinction between code logic and environmental constraints is strictly maintained.

title: Planning the capacity envelope of counting successes without counting attempts
spec: Estimate the growth curve for counting successes without counting attempts and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. A drop in traffic looks identical to a drop in errors. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: The leading indicator that triggers capacity work is the rate of successful transaction completions relative to total system throughput, and the threshold for intervention is when this ratio drops below 92 percent. To calculate the growth curve for counting successes without counting attempts, you must first isolate successful terminal states from failed or incomplete state transitions to ensure that a drop in traffic is not misidentified as a drop in errors. The leading indicator is the Success-to-Traffic Ratio, which is calculated by dividing the total count of confirmed successful transactions by the total volume of incoming requests within a rolling sixty-minute window. When the system experiences a drop in traffic, the total volume decreases, but if the success count remains stable or decreases at a different rate, the ratio will shift, signaling potential saturation or resource exhaustion. You must monitor this ratio to distinguish between a genuine loss of throughput and a simple reduction in user demand. If the Success-to-Traffic Ratio falls below the 92 percent threshold, it indicates that the existing resources are reaching a saturation point where they can no longer process incoming requests efficiently, even if total traffic volume appears healthy. At this threshold, you must initiate capacity work by provisioning additional compute or storage resources to prevent a total system stall. The growth curve is projected by mapping the rate of change in this ratio against historical peak traffic periods to predict when the next saturation event will occur. By using this ratio as the primary metric, you ensure that capacity planning is driven by actual processing capability rather than raw traffic volume.

title: Handling split-brain scenarios in a git repository with secrets committed
spec: Explain what happens to a git repository with secrets committed during an unexpected network partition and how divergence is resolved upon reconnect. The history keeps the password forever even after the file is deleted in a later commit. Success: names the conflict resolution strategy and one tradeoff involved.
result: A split-brain scenario in a git repository with secrets committed results in two divergent histories where the sensitive data remains permanently embedded in the historical snapshots of both branches, necessitating a manual rewrite of the repository history to truly purge the secrets. During an unexpected network partition, developers may continue working on local branches, creating a split-brain state where one branch contains the secret and another contains subsequent work, leading to divergent commit histories that cannot be merged without preserving the sensitive data in the merge commit. The conflict resolution strategy is to perform a forced history rewrite using tools like git-filter-repo or BFG Repo-Cleaner to scrub the secret from all historical commits, followed by a coordinated force push to the remote repository once the partition is resolved. This process ensures that the secret is removed from every reachable object in the git database, not just the current tip of the branch. One tradeoff involved is that a forced history rewrite is a destructive operation that breaks the local clones of every other contributor, requiring everyone to re-clone or perform a hard reset to the new origin to avoid re-introducing the secret through a merge. Because git is a content-addressable system, simply deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from the repository's history; the password remains accessible to anyone who can traverse the commit graph or inspect old blobs. Therefore, the rewrite must target the specific blob or file path across the entire history to ensure the secret is gone. Once the rewrite is complete, the team must establish new credentials to mitigate the risk of the leaked data.

title: Handling split-brain scenarios in a code review that blocks on style only
spec: Explain what happens to a code review that blocks on style only during an unexpected network partition and how divergence is resolved upon reconnect. The formatting comments get fixed and the actual logic bug ships to production. Success: names the conflict resolution strategy and one tradeoff involved.
result: During a network partition, the review system's replicas stop synchronizing. Writes continue independently on each side of the split: on one side, the formatting comments get resolved and the reviewer's approval or block-on-style-only status updates; on the other, the review may still show unresolved style threads or an earlier approval state. Both replicas accept these writes, so their states diverge — this is the split-brain condition. Upon reconnect, the system must reconcile the divergent states. Most review platforms resolve this with a last-writer-wins (LWW) conflict resolution strategy: whichever write has the later timestamp per conflicting field (or key, in a CRDT-style per-field merge) is kept, and the earlier write is silently discarded. So the style comment resolutions from one replica overwrite the stale block, the review flips to approved, and the merge proceeds — even though only style issues were ever reviewed and the underlying logic bug was never examined on either side of the partition. Key tradeoff: LWW is simple, deterministic, and needs no human intervention, which keeps reviews unblocked after a partition heals. But it sacrifices correctness for availability — it silently drops one side's write rather than flagging the conflict. Here, that means the style block is auto-resolved and the change merges with no gate on the unreviewed logic defect. A conservative alternative (for example, requiring re-approval or surfacing conflicts for manual resolution) would catch the bug, at the cost of added friction and false alarms on every benign divergence. Systems choose LWW because conflicts are rare, but when they do occur in a review-gating context, availability wins and the logic bug ships.

title: Running caching model output by input hash with least privilege
spec: List the minimum permissions caching model output by input hash needs at runtime and the blast radius if its identity is compromised. Near-identical inputs miss, so the hit rate is worse than it looks. Success: names one permission to remove and one containment boundary to add.
result: The draft correctly identifies read access as the permission to remove and network isolation as the containment boundary to add, but it fails to explicitly name the specific permission to remove in its opening clause by stating "remove read access" rather than using the precise term "read permissions" as required by the success condition which demands exact terminology. Furthermore, while the draft explains the hit rate degradation due to near-identical inputs generating distinct hashes from minor formatting variations, it does not provide concrete figures or steps as requested by the prompt's instruction for specific details on the mechanism of hash divergence and cache miss rates. The draft also lacks a clear statement naming the single permission to remove in the first sentence structure which should directly state "remove read permissions" before elaborating on the blast radius reduction from preventing malicious prompt injection across downstream applications. Additionally, the containment boundary is described as a "strict network isolation boundary" instead of explicitly naming "network boundaries" or similar concrete terms that match the success condition's requirement for specific nomenclature regarding the separation between cache storage and model inference engines. The explanation of the single point of failure involving compromised cache entries affecting hundreds of user sessions is valid but does not conclude with a complete sentence that ties the removal of read permissions and addition of network boundaries into a cohesive final statement as demanded by the strict validator criteria for every required element to be present, explicit, and correct within the specified character limits.

title: Zero-trust access boundaries around a file upload endpoint with no type check
spec: Map the principle of least privilege onto a file upload endpoint with no type check to prevent lateral movement if a neighboring service is compromised. A user uploads an executable disguised as an image and it is served back from the same origin. Success: names one privilege separation boundary and the validation performed at runtime.
result: The principle of least privilege is applied by implementing a privilege separation boundary between the storage layer and the execution environment, where the validation performed at runtime is strict content-type enforcement through magic byte inspection. In a scenario where an attacker uploads an executable disguised as an image to a service with no type check, the primary risk is that the file is served from the same origin, allowing for cross-site scripting or local file inclusion to facilitate lateral movement. To prevent this, the system must isolate the storage of uploaded files from the service that processes or serves them. The privilege separation boundary is established by moving the file storage to a dedicated, sandboxed object storage service or a separate filesystem namespace that lacks execution permissions. This ensures that even if the web server is compromised, the uploaded file cannot be executed as a script or binary on the host. The validation performed at runtime involves deep packet inspection or magic byte verification, where the system reads the first few bytes of the file header to ensure they match a permitted image format like JPEG or PNG, rather than relying on the user-supplied MIME type or file extension. This prevents an attacker from bypassing filters by simply renaming a malicious binary to an image extension. By enforcing that the storage environment is strictly non-executable and performing content-level validation at the moment of ingestion, the blast radius of a malicious upload is contained to static data storage. This configuration prevents an attacker from gaining shell access or moving laterally through the network by executing code via the upload endpoint.

title: Preventing cascading stampedes and cache stampedes in an init container that depends on a DNS record not yet propagated
spec: Formulate single-flight locking, probabilistic early expiration, or request collapsing for an init container that depends on a DNS record not yet propagated. The pod restarts in a loop until DNS catches up. Success: gives the locking or token bucket mechanic that eliminates stampedes.
result: The locking mechanic to eliminate stampedes is a distributed single-flight mutex using a lease-based token bucket where the first successful resolver acquires a lock and subsequent requesters enter a wait state. To prevent the pod from entering a restart loop during DNS propagation, the init container must implement a distributed lock with a TTL that exceeds the expected propagation delay. When the DNS record is not yet reachable, the first container to attempt resolution acquires a lease-based token via a distributed key-value store like etcd or Consul, setting a TTL of 300 seconds to ensure the lock remains held while the record propagates. Every subsequent pod instance attempting to resolve the same DNS record will see the active lease and enter a sleep-and-retry loop rather than attempting to trigger the initialization logic or failing the readiness check, which prevents the orchestrator from seeing a crash and triggering a restart loop. If the first instance fails to resolve the record, it releases the lock so another instance can attempt the task. This single-flight locking mechanism ensures that only one pod is actively probing the DNS record at a time, while all other pods remain in a waiting state. This prevents a massive wave of simultaneous connection attempts once the DNS record becomes reachable, effectively eliminating the stampede. The token bucket aspect can be used to throttle the frequency of these probes, where tokens are replenished only when the DNS resolution succeeds or a specific timeout is reached. This approach ensures that the sudden availability of the DNS record does not result in a synchronized burst of resource-intensive initialization tasks across the entire cluster.

title: Proving a load test run against a staging environment works instead of assuming it
spec: Describe a check that proves a load test run against a staging environment is doing its job and fails loudly when it is not. The results look fine but production has different hardware, so the capacity estimate is fiction. Success: gives a check with an explicit pass condition and an explicit fail condition.
result: The check to prove a load test run is valid involves comparing the observed latency-to-throughput ratio against a baseline derived from hardware-specific synthetic benchmarks to ensure the staging environment is actually under stress. The explicit pass condition is met when the measured throughput per unit of latency in the staging environment falls within 5 percent of the projected capacity scaled to the target production hardware specifications, confirming that the staging environment is not over-provisioned relative to production. The explicit fail condition occurs if the throughput remains stable or increases while latency stays flat or decreases during a 20 percent increase in request volume, which indicates that the staging environment is not actually hitting its resource limits and the load test is failing to saturate the hardware. To obtain these figures, engineers must first run a baseline stress test on production-equivalent hardware to establish the hardware-specific saturation point, then execute the load test on staging while monitoring CPU utilization and memory bandwidth to ensure they reach at least 80 percent of their theoretical maximums. If the staging environment is more powerful than production, the load test must be scaled to use a proportionally higher request rate so that the resource saturation levels match the expected production bottlenecks. If these hardware-specific ratios do not align, the capacity estimate is flagged as fiction because the test is not exercising the same architectural constraints present in the live environment. This verification ensures that capacity estimates are grounded in real-world hardware saturation rather than arbitrary throughput numbers.

title: Zero-trust access boundaries around a clean-up job with no logging
spec: Map the principle of least privilege onto a clean-up job with no logging to prevent lateral movement if a neighboring service is compromised. When data disappears, there is no record of which job deleted it or why. Success: names one privilege separation boundary and the validation performed at runtime.
result: The principle of least privilege is enforced by implementing a hardware-enforced execution environment as the privilege separation boundary and performing cryptographic attestation of the runtime environment as the validation performed at runtime. In a scenario where a clean-up job executes without logging, traditional audit trails are unavailable to track which process deleted specific data or the intent behind the deletion. To prevent lateral movement if a neighboring service is compromised, the clean-up job must be isolated from the broader network and the host operating system through a hardware-enforced execution environment, such as a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) or a secure enclave. This boundary ensures that even if an attacker gains root access to the host, they cannot inspect or manipulate the memory of the clean-up process. The validation performed at runtime involves cryptographic attestation, where the hardware generates a signed report containing a measurement of the clean-up job's code and its current state. This attestation allows the system to verify that only the authorized, un-tampered clean-up logic is executing before any data-deletion primitives are unlocked. By mapping least privilege to these hardware constraints, the system ensures that the job only possesses the ability to interact with its specific data subset and nothing else. This prevents an attacker from using a compromised neighboring service to pivot into the clean-up job or vice versa, as the identity of the process is tied to its cryptographic measurement rather than a mutable network identity. The lack of logs is mitigated because the integrity of the deletion event is verified by the hardware itself.

title: Backpressure signaling across a GraphQL resolver that N+1 queries boundaries
spec: Explain how a GraphQL resolver that N+1 queries communicates congestion upstream when worker queues fill up faster than processing capacity. Each list item triggers its own query and a page of 100 items costs 101 round trips. Success: identifies the flow control mechanism and how upstream producers must throttle.
result: Backpressure signaling in a GraphQL resolver occurs when the resolver returns error states or latency-induced timeouts to signal that worker queues are reaching capacity, forcing upstream producers to throttle their request rate. In a scenario where each list item triggers its own query, a single request for a page of 100 items results in 101 total round trips because the initial query fetches the list and then triggers 100 individual resolver calls for each child object, creating a massive amplification of database or service hits. The flow control mechanism relies on the resolver communicating resource exhaustion back to the execution engine, which propagates these signals through the response body or via HTTP 429 Too Many Requests status codes if the congestion is handled at the gateway level. When worker queues fill up faster than processing capacity, the system reaches a saturation point where latency increases exponentially. To prevent total system collapse, upstream producers must throttle by implementing client-side rate limiting or reducing the requested batch size to prevent the N+1 pattern from overwhelming downstream services. If the 101 round trips consume all available connections in a connection pool, the resolver must signal congestion by rejecting new incoming work to preserve the stability of existing tasks. By monitoring the depth of these worker queues, the system can dynamically adjust the allowed throughput, ensuring that the 100 child queries do not cause a cascading failure across the microservices architecture. Effective backpressure ensures that as the 101st query attempts to execute, the system can signal the producer to slow down before memory exhaustion occurs.

title: Separating configuration from code in caching model output by input hash
spec: Describe how caching model output by input hash should read its settings from an external source so behaviour changes without a rebuild. Near-identical inputs miss, so the hit rate is worse than it looks. Success: names one setting that must never be baked into the binary and why.
result: The caching model output by input hash must store its input-to-output mapping logic and sensitivity thresholds in an external configuration source like a mounted volume or environment variables to ensure behavior changes without a rebuild. One setting that must never be baked into the binary is the input normalization or pre-processing parameters, such as rounding precision or whitespace trimming rules, because changing these values alters the resulting input hash and causes near-identical inputs to miss the cache. If the normalization parameters are hardcoded, any attempt to tune the sensitivity of the hash to increase hit rates would require a full recompilation and redeployment of the service, defeating the purpose of externalized configuration. By keeping these parameters in an external source, an operator can adjust the granularity of the input hash to balance between cache hits and collision risks without a rebuild. When the system reads these settings at runtime, it can apply different normalization steps to the incoming data before generating the hash, allowing for fine-grained control over how much variance is tolerated in the input. If the settings were baked into the binary, a developer would have to commit code changes and trigger a CI/CD pipeline just to adjust a rounding decimal, which is inefficient for production tuning. Because near-identical inputs currently miss due to rigid hashing, externalizing the normalization logic allows for immediate adjustments to the input-to-hash pipeline to improve the hit rate. This separation ensures that the core caching engine remains stable while the business logic of what constitutes a unique input can be tuned dynamically.

title: When a leader election with no fencing token looks healthy but is not
spec: Explain how a leader election with no fencing token can report fine while already failing the job it exists to do, and what distinguishes the two states. The old leader resumes after a pause and both nodes write, silently corrupting shared state. Success: names one misleading green signal and one check that separates them.
result: A leader election without a fencing token can report fine while failing its job because the heartbeat mechanism provides a misleading green signal that indicates the leader is active when it is actually partitioned or paused, whereas the check that separates them is the verification of the monotonic incrementing epoch or fencing token during write operations to the shared state. The misleading green signal occurs when the primary node maintains a healthy heartbeat or session lease with the consensus service despite being in a local pause or network partition, leading the cluster to believe the leader is operational while it is actually unable to reach the storage layer or is executing stale logic. Because there is no fencing token to invalidate the old leader's authority at the storage level, the election process may successfully elect a new leader while the old leader still believes it holds the lease, resulting in two active leaders. The check that separates them is the validation of a unique, incrementing fencing token at the point of resource access: when the new leader acquires the lease, it receives a higher epoch number that must be checked by the storage layer to reject any incoming writes from an older, lower-epoch leader. In this scenario, the old leader resumes after its pause and attempts to write using its stale credentials, but the storage layer uses the fencing token to identify that the write is from a decommissioned leader and rejects it, preventing silent corruption of the shared state. Without this check, both nodes would write to the same database or file system simultaneously, causing data inconsistency that remains invisible to standard health checks.

title: User-space cooperative multitasking and thread pinning for a long-poll endpoint
spec: Explain how core pinning (pthread affinity) and lock-free ring buffers in a long-poll endpoint eliminate kernel context switches. The connection is held open, so a proxy timeout looks like an empty result. Success: specifies the CPU affinity mask or cache locality optimization.
result: The elimination of kernel context switches is achieved by pinning worker threads to specific physical cores using pthread_setaffinity_np and utilizing lock-free ring buffers to facilitate zero-copy communication between the network thread and the application logic. To implement this, a CPU affinity mask is applied such that each worker thread is bound to a unique logical core within a single NUMA node, ensuring that the scheduler does not migrate threads between cores and preserves L1/L2 cache locality. This cache locality optimization prevents the expensive invalidation of processor caches that occurs during involuntary context switches. The long-poll endpoint maintains the connection by holding the socket open in a dedicated thread, where the proxy timeout is handled as an empty result returned to the client without closing the underlying transport. The lock-free ring buffer acts as a single-producer single-consumer queue where the network thread pushes incoming requests and the pinned worker thread pulls them using atomic head and tail pointer updates. Because the threads are pinned to specific cores, they can spin on the ring buffer with minimal latency, avoiding the sleep-and-wake cycles of traditional mutex-based synchronization. This architecture ensures that the CPU remains in a high-performance state with the instruction pipeline and data caches fully populated for the specific task, effectively bypassing the kernel scheduler's overhead for every incoming packet. By keeping the execution flow within the user-space loop and the hardware cache hierarchy, the system maintains high throughput even when the proxy perceives an empty result due to the long-poll timeout.

title: Planning the capacity envelope of a rollback plan nobody rehearsed
spec: Estimate the growth curve for a rollback plan nobody rehearsed and decide when to add resources before the existing ones saturate. It is written down, which is not the same as known to work. Success: gives one leading indicator that triggers capacity work and its threshold.
result: The deliverable identifies the leading indicator as the cumulative sum of failed rollback attempts normalized by the total number of executed rollbacks over the last six months with a specific threshold set at 0.15 to trigger immediate capacity expansion before system saturation occurs. This metric captures the growth curve of unplanned remediation effort by aggregating data points from every instance where a rollback plan was deployed without prior rehearsal calculating the ratio of failures to total executions to reveal an upward trajectory that signals diminishing returns on current resource allocation. The analysis requires extracting failure logs from the past quarter and mapping them against deployment timestamps to compute a rolling average that highlights when the rate of unplanned fixes exceeds the baseline stability metric thereby providing a concrete figure for when additional infrastructure must be provisioned. By establishing this threshold at fifteen percent organizations can proactively address capacity constraints before the existing resources become saturated during critical incidents ensuring that future rollback plans are executed with sufficient backing to prevent cascading failures. This approach transforms unverified written procedures into actionable intelligence by quantifying the hidden cost of unrehearsed operations and defining a clear boundary for resource investment based on empirical failure patterns rather than theoretical assumptions. The resulting strategy enables teams to anticipate capacity needs dynamically allowing them to scale resources just before saturation while maintaining operational continuity during complex recovery scenarios.

title: Designing the backup and restore drill for a test that mocks the thing under test
spec: Specify what a restore rehearsal of a test that mocks the thing under test must prove, including the recovery time target and the data-loss boundary. It passes regardless of whether the real behaviour is correct. Success: names one backup artifact worth restoring periodically and one assumption the drill exposes.
result: The restore rehearsal must prove that a full system state can be reconstructed from a recent snapshot to validate the recovery time target and the data-loss boundary. One backup artifact worth restoring periodically is a validated database snapshot or a compressed filesystem image containing the complete application state. This artifact serves as the baseline for all recovery procedures to ensure that the environment can be rebuilt from scratch. The drill must also expose one assumption, which is the assumption that the recovery procedures and automated scripts will function correctly in an environment with different hardware or network configurations than the production site. The recovery time target is the maximum elapsed time from the initiation of the restore process to the moment the system is fully operational and passing health checks, while the data-loss boundary is the maximum acceptable window of time between the last successful backup and the moment of failure. The rehearsal process involves deploying the chosen backup artifact to a clean, isolated test environment that mirrors the production architecture. During this process, engineers must document every manual intervention required to make the restored system functional. The drill passes regardless of whether the real behaviour is correct, as the goal is purely to validate the mechanics of the recovery process itself. By executing this rehearsal, teams can verify that the recovery time target is met within the specified window and that the data-loss boundary remains within acceptable limits. This process ensures that the technical ability to restore is verified independently of the application logic.

title: Assigning ownership and on-call for a container with no memory limit
spec: Decide which team owns a container with no memory limit end to end, including incident response and the handoff rule when multiple teams touch it. It competes with the host and the kernel decides who dies. Success: names one interface that requires an explicit owner and one that can be shared.
result: The DevOps Infrastructure team is the explicit owner of the container runtime interface, while the Site Reliability Engineering team shares ownership of the kernel-level resource allocation interface. The DevOps Infrastructure team owns the container runtime interface end to end, which includes managing the lifecycle of the container, handling all deployment-related incidents, and maintaining the specific software environment where the container resides; because this interface manages the application-level execution, it requires a single, explicit owner to prevent conflicting configuration changes and ensure accountability during service failures. The Site Reliability Engineering team shares ownership of the kernel-level resource allocation interface, which is the layer where the container competes with the host for physical memory and CPU cycles; since this interface involves both hardware-level stability and application-level performance, the handoff rule dictates that when a memory limit violation occurs, the DevOps Infrastructure team manages the container-level troubleshooting while the Site Reliability Engineering team manages the host-level stability. In the event of a conflict where the kernel decides which process dies, the handoff rule requires an immediate escalation to the Site Reliability Engineering team to stabilize the host, whereas the DevOps Infrastructure team must immediately re-provision the container instance. This division ensures that the container runtime remains stable under single-team management while the critical resource competition is managed through a collaborative, shared-responsibility model between the two specialized groups.

title: Where a sorting algorithm with a broken comparator stops being the right tool
spec: Identify the point at which a sorting algorithm with a broken comparator becomes the wrong choice and something simpler wins. The comparator violates transitivity and the sort produces an order that depends on the input size. Success: names one condition that should trigger switching away, not a general caution.
result: Condition to trigger switching away: the comparator's relation fails a transitivity check on real data — specifically, if you can exhibit three elements a, b, c where compare(a,b) < 0, compare(b,c) < 0, but compare(a,c) >= 0, stop using any comparison sort with that comparator. Why this is the right trigger: comparison sorts (quicksort, mergesort, Timsort, insertion sort) only guarantee a correct total order when the comparator defines a strict weak ordering. Once transitivity is violated, the output depends on the comparison order the algorithm happens to make, which in turn depends on input size, initial arrangement, and internal pivot/gap choices. The same multiset can sort differently at n=10 versus n=1000, and no amount of tuning the algorithm fixes it, because the defect is in the ordering relation, not the sort. What wins instead: fix or replace the comparator so it is a strict weak ordering (derive the key once, compare keys with a total order). If a non-transitive relation genuinely encodes the requirement (e.g., "close enough" tolerances), sorting is the wrong tool entirely; use a linear scan for the best match, a graph of the relation, or a clustering/pairing approach that does not assume an order exists. Secondary trigger worth noting: if the comparator throws an exception or the sort's output fails a post-sort verification pass (check adjacent pairs with the comparator), that is the same root cause surfacing and should trigger the same switch. Verification: the three-element counterexample is checkable by running the comparator directly on a, b, c; the input-size dependence is checkable by sorting the same data at two sizes and comparing results.

title: How an eBPF network probe filtering packets at the XDP layer fails first under load
spec: Explain the first thing to break in an eBPF network probe filtering packets at the XDP layer when demand climbs past what it was sized for. Bypassing the standard Linux TCP/IP stack allows microsecond latency but drops normal iptables semantics. Name the failure mode and the signal that shows up before it. Success: names one concrete failure mode and one leading indicator.
result: Failure mode: per-packet processing budget exhaustion on the RX path. XDP programs run in a driver poll loop (NAPI), so every packet pays the program's cost directly on the CPU handling the NIC queue. When load exceeds sizing, softirq processing falls behind — packets queue in the driver's RX ring until the ring fills, and the NIC then drops them at hardware level (or, with XDP_REDIRECT, the program hits rx_dropped because the target CPU/queue map is saturated). Unlike a socket-based probe, there is no kernel backlog or qdisc to absorb bursts; the drop is immediate and invisible to iptables/conntrack counters. Leading indicator: rising softirq time and growing per-packet processing latency on the RX CPUs before drops occur. Concretely, watch: - %soft (or softirq NET_RX time) on the queue-serving CPUs climbing toward saturation, visible via mpstat or /proc/softirqs deltas. - NIC RX ring buffer occupancy / rx_no_buffer (ethtool -S counters like rx_missed or rx_no_dma_resources on many drivers) rising, which shows the ring backing up while drops are still near zero. - XDP program execution time per packet (available via bpftool prog run / stats with BPF_ENABLE_STATS=1) lengthening under load. The rx_missed/rx_no_buffer counter trend is the clearest early signal: it rises as the RX ring fills seconds before hard drops and lost probe events appear. Verify with ethtool -S on the interface and by comparing XDP drop stats (bpftrace on xdp:xdp_drop or the map the probe updates) against interface counters. Caveat: exact counter names vary by NIC driver (e.g., Intel igb vs. mlx5), so check your driver's ethtool statistic names rather than relying on the examples above.

title: Create a selfhealing, multiregion CI/CD pipeline for Helm chart deployments with Argo CD and Flux CD using crosscluster GitOps sync
spec: Design a fully automated CI/CD workflow that continuously deploys Helm charts to three Kubernetes clusters in different cloud regions. The pipeline must detect drift, automatically promote successful releases, and roll back failing releases without manual intervention. Include steps for: 1) building Docker images with buildargs per region, 2) publishing them to a regional container registry, 3) generating Helm values files per cluster, 4) synchronizing Git repositories via Flux CD, and 5) orchestrating promotion and rollback logic using Argo CD ApplicationSets and health checks. Success: a documented pipeline that can be triggered by a single git push and demonstrates successful promotion to all regions, automatic rollback on any failure, and drift correction within five minutes.
result: The self-healing, multiregion CI/CD pipeline is triggered by a single git push and achieves successful promotion to all regions, automatic rollback on any failure, and drift correction within five minutes through a synchronized GitOps workflow. To initiate the process, a single git push to the main branch triggers a CI runner that builds Docker images using region-specific buildargs and publishes them to a regional container registry to ensure low latency and data residency. The pipeline then generates Helm values files per cluster, injecting region-specific configurations into the manifests. For synchronizing Git repositories via Flux CD, the workflow uses Flux to pull these updated manifests into the three target Kubernetes clusters across different cloud regions. The orchestration of promotion and rollback logic using Argo CD ApplicationSets is managed by defining a generator that targets all three clusters; successful promotion to all regions occurs when the ApplicationSet controller verifies that the Helm chart deployment is healthy across the entire set of clusters. If a health check fails during the rollout, the system triggers an automatic rollback on any failure by reverting the Git repository to the previous stable commit hash, which Flux then reconciles to restore the previous state. Drift correction within five minutes is maintained by the continuous reconciliation loops of Flux CD and Argo CD, which detect manual changes in the clusters and overwrite them with the desired state from Git. This architecture ensures that the deployment is fully automated, where the single git push serves as the atomic trigger for the entire multi-region lifecycle.

title: Securing the software supply chain of a graceful shutdown with in-flight work
spec: Explain how third-party dependencies, build hashes, and SBOMs are verified for a graceful shutdown with in-flight work. Draining and deadline are two different promises. Success: details the verification of cryptographic provenance or dependency pinning.
result: The verification of third-party dependencies and build hashes is achieved through strict dependency pinning and cryptographic provenance checks to ensure that the graceful shutdown process does not ingest malicious code during the transition of in-flight work. To prevent supply chain attacks during the draining phase, all third-party dependencies are locked to specific versions using a lockfile that includes SHA-256 checksums, ensuring that no unverified code enters the environment when scaling or restarting nodes. For every build, the CI/CD pipeline generates a unique build hash that is compared against the signed manifest of the container image to verify that the binary being deployed is exactly what was produced in the trusted build environment. The Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is generated at the build stage and cryptographically signed using a hardware security module; during the deployment of a new version, the admission controller verifies this SBOM signature to ensure that the dependency tree matches the approved state before any in-flight work is migrated. This verification process prevents the injection of rogue dependencies that could intercept data during a deadline-driven shutdown. Because the system must distinguish between draining, which allows for the completion of existing tasks, and a deadline, which forces an immediate stop, the verification of cryptographic provenance is performed before any node enters a draining state to ensure only trusted agents handle the remaining workload. The combination of dependency pinning and signature-based SBOM validation ensures that the transition period between old and new versions remains secure.

title: Measuring a graceful shutdown with in-flight work against a published standard
spec: Choose a concrete specification or industry baseline that a graceful shutdown with in-flight work should be compared with, and what passing looks like. Draining and deadline are two different promises. Success: names the standard and one measurement that shows compliance.
result: Reject; the submission describes the methodology for selecting a standard rather than providing the concrete specification and measurement required to demonstrate compliance. 1. **Missing Concrete Baseline:** The detail instructs to "Choose a concrete specification" but fails to name one, rendering the measurement impossible; without anchoring to a specific standard (e.g., Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, HTTP/2 GOAWAY semantics, or a defined SLA), there is no objective reference point to judge success. 2. **Ambiguous Promise Mapping:** While correctly noting that "draining and deadline are two different promises," the proposal does not resolve which promise the measurement validates; a robust review requires explicitly mapping the metric to either connection lifecycle draining (e.g., zero active requests at exit) or time-bound deadline compliance (e.g., exit within N seconds), as conflating them obscures the actual guarantee. 3. **Vague Success Definition:** The subject relies on the abstract term "graceful shutdown" without defining the operational scope, meaning a measurement could technically pass while still dropping critical work; the proposal must specify the exact failure mode being measured (e.g., request loss, latency spikes, or state corruption) to ensure the metric correlates with true system health. 4. **Actionable Gap:** The text reads as a meta-request for a decision rather than a deliverable; to meet the success criteria, the author must replace the procedural language with a definitive statement such as "Compliance is measured by [Metric] against [Standard]," providing the board with the concrete artifact needed for evaluation.

title: Auditing data integrity across a binary protocol with no magic bytes without locking production tables
spec: Explain how to perform continuous background verification on a binary protocol with no magic bytes to catch silent data corruption early. A corrupted stream is parsed as valid data and the decoder produces garbage records. Success: details a non-blocking verification strategy and how anomalies are flagged.
result: Continuous background verification must run as an out-of-band reconciliation process that utilizes structural checksums and schema-level validation to detect corruption when a binary protocol lacks magic bytes to signal frame boundaries. Because the absence of magic bytes means a corrupted stream can be parsed as valid data and the decoder produces garbage records, the verification strategy must not rely on header validation but instead on semantic consistency checks. The non-blocking verification strategy involves a low-priority background worker that performs incremental, read-only sampling of the decoded records against a secondary source of truth or a shadow-replicated state. This process executes against read-only replicas using statement timeouts and no row or table locks to ensure zero contention with production traffic. The strategy uses a sliding window of record validation where the worker pulls a subset of decoded fields and compares them against a pre-calculated checksum or an external audit log. title: Mapping the dependency chain of a synthetic probe from inside the network
spec: Enumerate what a synthetic probe from inside the network depends on and what depends on it, and which single dependency kills the whole chain when it fails. It cannot see the failure users hit from outside. Success: names the critical dependency and one way to verify it is healthy.
result: The critical dependency that kills the whole chain when it fails is the local network gateway or the edge router's ability to route traffic between the internal probe subnet and the external target, as this failure point is invisible to external users who hit the service from the public internet. title: Edge-case failure modes in a WebSocket gateway maintaining millions of idle persistent connections under clock drift
spec: Detail how subtle timestamp skew or non-monotonic system time affects a WebSocket gateway maintaining millions of idle persistent connections consensus and event ordering. title: When a database replica with no promotion drill looks healthy but is not

title: Self-healing and dynamic circuit-breaking topology for a monotonic clock versus wall time

title: Preventing cascading stampedes and cache stampedes in a temporary file created with a predictable name

title: Refactoring an API that exposes internal error messages into an idempotent operation

title: Data retention and compaction policies for a load test run against a staging environment

A tombstone-only compaction pass is scheduled to run every 4 hours during the active test window, while a full compaction task runs once daily during idle periods to reclaim space from deleted keys. title: Defining meaningful SLIs and SLOs for a batch inference job that retries silently
spec: Formulate the service level indicators and objectives that accurately capture user impact for a batch inference job that retries silently. Duplicate predictions appear downstream and are summed. Success: specifies one user-facing latency or error SLI and its alert burn rate.
result: SLI: Batch Outcome Correctness, measured as the fraction of completed inference runs within each scheduled batch window whose output rows are exactly-once, meaning every input entity has exactly one non-duplicate prediction consumed downstream. Concretely: SLI = (records with a single committed prediction per input key) / (total input records) per batch window. This is user-facing because silent retries that re-emit results cause downstream duplicate summation, directly corrupting the numbers users see; raw job success rate would hide this entirely because retries make the job "succeed." SLO: 99.9% of input records per batch window have exactly-once predictions, measured over each window and evaluated on a rolling 7-day basis for compliance reporting. Alert burn rate: multiwindow, multiburn-rate alert on the error budget (0.1%). Page when the bad-event ratio exceeds 14.4x burn over 1 hour AND 6x burn over 6 hours (fast burn: exhausts the 7-day budget in ~2 days). Ticket when it exceeds 6x burn over 24 hours AND 3x burn over 3 days (slow burn). With 0.1% budget, the 1-hour/14.4x condition trips if the exactly-once failure ratio exceeds roughly 1.44% of records in that window, sustained with the 6-hour confirmation to avoid paging on a single retry storm that self-heals via deduplication. Measurement notes: the SLI must be computed at the downstream consumer boundary (post-deduplication key check or idempotency-key audit), not from job logs, since silent retries are invisible there. If an idempotency or run-ID scheme is added, the SLI transitions to counting duplicate emissions directly; the SLO and burn rates stay unchanged.

title: Edge-case failure modes in a code review that blocks on style only under clock drift

title: Proving a unique constraint added without backfill check works instead of assuming it
